screeningScope: Full-text source, eligibility, taxonomy, and synthesis-readiness review of Nutrition & Hydration shortlist positions 49-60.

decisionDefinitions.INCLUDE: Eligible for evidence extraction and synthesis after full-text review.
decisionDefinitions.DEGRADED: A required source or verification element was unavailable.

records.sourceFile: The Effect of Multi-Ingredient Protein versus Collagen Supplementation on Satellite Cell Properties in Males and Females.pdf
records.evidenceSummary: Twenty-six adults completed 10 weeks of resistance training while twice daily consuming multi-ingredient whey, creatine, leucine, calcium, and vitamin-D supplementation or collagen. The multi-ingredient group had greater type-II fiber cross-sectional-area gain, but satellite-cell content, myonuclear accretion, and most acute satellite-cell responses were similar.
records.limitations: The small mixed-sex sample and multi-ingredient comparison prevent attribution to protein alone. Most differences were not statistically robust, biopsies measured mechanistic markers rather than sport outcomes, and collagen was not an inert control.
records.synthesisCaution: Do not generalize a multi-ingredient supplement result into a required muscle-repair product. Food intake, training, total protein, tolerance, and ingredient-specific safety require individual review.

records.sourceFile: An association between bioavailable 25-hydroxyvitamin D and bone mineral density in a diverse cohort of collegiate athletes.pdf
records.evidenceSummary: In 53 Division-I basketball and swimming athletes, total and bioavailable 25-hydroxyvitamin D categorized many participants differently, especially Black athletes. Bioavailable 25-hydroxyvitamin D correlated positively with total bone mineral density (r=0.618), whereas total 25-hydroxyvitamin D did not.
records.limitations: This small cross-sectional sample cannot establish that vitamin-D exposure changes bone density or outcomes. It included two sports at one setting, and calculated bioavailability and classification cutoffs require clinical context.
records.synthesisCaution: Use vitamin-D assessment and bone-health decisions with qualified clinical and nutrition staff; do not infer supplementation need, fracture prevention, or superiority of one marker from this association alone.

records.sourceFile: Inside the belly of a Beast - Individualizing nutrition for young professional male Rugby League players - A review.pdf
records.evidenceSummary: This review proposes rugby-league nutrition targets from the limited sport-specific evidence: approximately 6-8 g/kg/day carbohydrate, 1.6-2.6 g/kg/day protein, and 0.7-2.2 g/kg/day fat, with phase-specific pre- and postexercise carbohydrate and protein strategies. It notes that young professional rugby-league energy expenditure and requirements need further measurement.
records.limitations: It is a narrative review, and many recommendations are extrapolated rather than rugby-league-specific. Female athletes, individual energy expenditure, body-composition goals, and season phase variation are inadequately characterized.
records.synthesisCaution: Use these numbers only as starting ranges for individualized planning, not fixed prescriptions. Monitor body mass, training demand, recovery, gastrointestinal tolerance, health, and food access.

records.sourceFile: UEFA expert group statement on nutrition in elite football - Current evidence to inform practical recommendations and guide future research.pdf
records.evidenceSummary: The UEFA expert statement recommends a food-first, individualized and periodized approach to nutrition, fluids, and evidence-based supplements in elite soccer. It emphasizes matching intake to training and match demands while considering health, body composition, travel, recovery, practical feasibility, and antidoping risk.
records.limitations: It is expert consensus synthesizing evidence of uneven quality rather than a single controlled trial. Elite-soccer recommendations may not transfer to collegiate, youth, female, or other-sport settings without contextual adjustment.
records.synthesisCaution: Use the statement as an integrated planning framework, not as a rigid menu or supplement list. Individual energy availability, medical needs, culture, travel, and qualified practitioner oversight remain decisive.

records.sourceFile: Blood, Sweat. and Tears - Implications for Hydration Testing in Combat Sports - Investigating Body Mass Loss and Biomarker Changes.pdf
records.evidenceSummary: Fifteen combat-sport athletes completed two sauna-dehydration trials targeting 4% body-mass loss and averaged 3.0%. Body-mass loss explained hematocrit change but not serum or urine osmolality or other markers; post-dehydration hematocrit had the strongest reliability, while conventional urine-specific-gravity cutoff 1.020 misclassified 42%.
records.limitations: The small sample used passive sauna dehydration, achieved less than the target loss, and may not represent competition weight-cutting or field testing. Biomarker reliability and cutoff performance depend on timing and the tested cohort.
records.synthesisCaution: Do not rely on one hydration test or cutoff to clear combat athletes. Hydration policies should use validated context-specific protocols and prioritize health, monitoring, and safe weight-management practices.

records.sourceFile: The Association of Vitamin D Status              in Lower Extremity Muscle Strains and Core Muscle Injuries at   the          National   Football League Combine.pdf
records.evidenceSummary: At the 2015 NFL Combine, 214 athletes had vitamin-D data and retrospective injury histories. Inadequate vitamin D was present in 59%; unadjusted analyses associated inadequate status with lower-extremity strain or core injury history and higher odds of hamstring history, but low vitamin D was not independently associated after multivariable adjustment.
records.limitations: This retrospective combine sample cannot determine temporality or causation, and injury histories and confounding factors limit interpretation. The adjusted result was not independently significant and it does not test supplementation.
records.synthesisCaution: Screening and supplementation decisions require clinical context and should not claim that low vitamin D caused a past strain or will prevent a future one.

records.sourceFile: Effects of Protein Supplementation During Early Rehabilitation on Muscle Volume and Function After Acute Muscle Strain Injuries - A Randomized Controlled Trial.pdf
records.evidenceSummary: Fifty recreational athletes with acute hamstring or calf strains received twice-daily whey protein or isocaloric placebo during early rehabilitation. Injured-muscle volume fell about 9.4% and remained lower at 12 months; protein did not improve volume, strength, return-to-sport time, or aponeurosis changes.
records.limitations: The recreational sample, injury heterogeneity, and early rehabilitation setting limit transfer to elite sport. The trial tests this whey protocol against placebo, not total dietary-protein adequacy or other nutrition interventions.
records.synthesisCaution: Do not present whey supplementation as a proven way to preserve muscle or speed return after muscle strain. Ensure adequate overall intake and integrate nutrition with progressive rehabilitation.

records.sourceFile: Position-Specific Longitudinal Assessment of Total and Regional Body Composition in NCAA Division I Football Players.pdf
records.degradedReason: The full-text source is readable and title-matched, but the manuscript PDF exposes no verifiable DOI. Publication-identity metadata is incomplete, so no public synthesis is prepared.

records.sourceFile: The effects of creatine supplementation on cognitive performance - A randomized controlled study.pdf
records.evidenceSummary: In a preregistered double-blind crossover trial, 123 vegetarians and omnivores took 5 g/day creatine and placebo for six weeks each. Bayesian analysis supported a small cognitive benefit; backward digit span bordered significance, Raven matrices and exploratory tests did not, vegetarians did not benefit more, and side effects were more frequent with creatine.
records.limitations: Participants were not an athlete-performance cohort, effects were small and task-specific, and the study cannot establish sport-cognition or concussion benefit. Side-effect reporting and individual response matter.
records.synthesisCaution: Do not recommend creatine for cognitive performance on this study alone. If used for other supported indications, discuss goals, tolerance, contraindications, and product quality with qualified staff.

records.sourceFile: Does Caffeine Supplementation Affect Sleep in Athletes - A Systematic Review of Nine Randomized Controlled trials.pdf
records.evidenceSummary: This review of nine randomized athlete trials evaluated caffeine and sleep. The authors report that caffeine can impair sleep measures, with effects depending on dose, timing, and individual sensitivity, and recommend balancing ergogenic use against recovery needs.
records.limitations: Only nine heterogeneous trials were available, with varied athlete samples, caffeine protocols, sleep measures, and study quality. The source is an accepted pre-proof, and evidence does not establish one universally safe timing or dose.
records.synthesisCaution: Plan caffeine around both performance and sleep opportunity; avoid assuming a standard dose or withdrawal window is harmless for every athlete.

records.sourceFile: Nutritional Supplement and Dietary Interventions as a Prophylaxis or Treatment of Sub-Concussive Repetitive Head Impact and Mild Traumatic Brain Injury - A Systematic Review.pdf
records.evidenceSummary: This systematic review included 15 studies from 12 subject populations and 1,139 participants with mild traumatic brain injury or repetitive head-impact exposure. Eleven studies reported benefit; omega-3 fatty acids, melatonin, and Pinus radiata had multiple studies, but the authors judged multicenter work necessary before firm efficacy conclusions.
records.limitations: Interventions, populations, timing, outcomes, and risk of bias varied; 53.3% of studies had at least some bias concern and industry-sponsored studies all reported supportive results. Evidence is insufficient to establish a clinical supplement protocol.
records.synthesisCaution: Do not treat supplements as concussion prevention or treatment. Follow medical concussion management and use nutrition only as adjunctive, clinically supervised support when evidence and athlete context warrant.

records.sourceFile: Can I have my coffee and drink it - A systematic review and meta-analysis to determine whether habitual caffeine consumption affects the ergogenic effect of caffeine.pdf
records.evidenceSummary: Sixty caffeine studies supplied habitual-consumption data. Caffeine improved performance versus placebo overall (SMD 0.25), and habitual consumption did not moderate the effect; benefits were seen below 3 and at 3-6 mg/kg, not above 6 mg/kg in subgroup analysis.
records.limitations: Habitual intake and body mass were usually group means, few studies directly tested habituation, caffeine estimates were imprecise, and no included study had low risk of bias. Findings do not resolve individual sleep, anxiety, cardiovascular, or sport-specific response.
records.synthesisCaution: Habitual use alone need not dictate caffeine efficacy, but individual trialing, sleep protection, timing, dose, adverse effects, and antidoping product review remain essential.
